o: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is L2, 3

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve comes from the posterior divisions of L2 and L3.
It supplies the lateral thigh.
The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve is L1

The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve is L1; the genital branch is L2.
A Last's detail.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is L5

The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is S2 (S1 to S3), not L5.
It supplies the back of the thigh.
The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve pierces sartorius near its origin

The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve pierces sartorius above its insertion. It is the intermediate cutaneous nerve of the thigh that pierces sartorius near its origin.
Two different nerves.

questions.s: Muscles with dual innervation in the thigh (Last's):
o: Pectineus

Pectineus has a dual supply: femoral and obturator (or accessory obturator).
It sits at the junction of two compartments.
Adductor magnus

Adductor magnus has a dual supply: the obturator nerve (adductor part) and the tibial part of the sciatic (hamstring part).
It is a hybrid muscle.
Biceps femoris

Biceps femoris has a dual supply: long head from the tibial part, short head from the common peroneal part.
The short head migrated from the extensor compartment.
Gracilis

Gracilis is supplied by the obturator nerve only.
It is a pure adductor compartment muscle.
The femoral artery always lies between the saphenous nerve and femoral vein

In the adductor canal the femoral artery always lies between the saphenous nerve and the femoral vein.
The nerve crosses in front of the artery.
The femoral vein lies lateral to the artery at the adductor hiatus

The femoral vein lies lateral to the artery at the adductor hiatus, having been medial at the femoral triangle.
It spirals around the artery.
The femoral vein lies medial to the artery at the hiatus

At the hiatus the femoral vein lies lateral to the artery, not medial.
Medial is its position in the femoral triangle.
The nerve to vastus medialis runs in the lower part of the canal

The nerve to vastus medialis runs in the upper part of the canal, not the lower.
It leaves early to enter the muscle.
The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the main contents

From superficial to deep in the popliteal fossa: tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery. So the nerve is most superficial.
The artery lies on the floor.
The popliteal vein lies between the artery and the nerve

The popliteal vein is sandwiched between the artery (deepest) and the tibial nerve (most superficial).
Last's emphasises this constant order.
The common peroneal nerve runs lateral to the biceps tendon

The common peroneal nerve runs medial to the biceps tendon, beneath the deep fascia, not lateral to it.
It then winds round the neck of the fibula.
The floor from above down is popliteus, capsule, femur

The floor of the popliteal fossa, from above down, is the femur (popliteal surface), the capsule of the knee, then popliteus.
The statement reverses the order.

questions.s: Structures piercing the roof of the popliteal fossa (Last's):
o: The small saphenous vein

The small saphenous vein pierces the roof of the popliteal fossa to join the popliteal vein.
Its termination varies.
The peroneal communicating nerve

The peroneal communicating nerve pierces the roof to join the sural nerve.
It comes from the common peroneal nerve.
The lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf pierces the roof over the lateral head of gastrocnemius.
Also from the common peroneal nerve.
The sural nerve

The sural nerve pierces the deep fascia halfway down the leg, not the roof of the popliteal fossa.
It runs deep to the fascia between the gastrocnemius heads first.

questions.s: Nerve supply of the knee joint (Last's):
o: The nerve to vastus medialis

The nerve to vastus medialis (femoral) supplies the knee joint.
Hilton's law.
The posterior division of the obturator nerve

The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies the knee, accompanying the femoral artery through the adductor hiatus.
Explains referred knee pain from the hip.
Genicular branches of the tibial nerve

Genicular branches of the tibial (and common peroneal) parts of the sciatic nerve supply the knee.
They accompany the genicular arteries.
The saphenous nerve proper

Last's does not list the saphenous nerve trunk itself as a nerve to the knee joint; its infrapatellar branch supplies the skin in front of the knee (some texts also credit it with a small articular twig).
Contrast ll question 19, which counts the infrapatellar branch.
The femoral nerve comes from posterior divisions of L2, 3, 4

The femoral nerve comes from the posterior divisions of L2, L3 and L4, so it supplies extensors (quadriceps).
Posterior divisions supply extensor muscles.
The obturator nerve comes from anterior divisions of L2, 3, 4

The obturator nerve comes from the anterior divisions of L2, L3 and L4 and supplies the adductors.
Anterior divisions supply flexor-type muscles.
The accessory obturator is present in about two-thirds

Last's says the accessory obturator nerve is present in about one-third of people, not two-thirds.
When present it supplies pectineus.
The accessory obturator nerve supplies adductor longus

The accessory obturator nerve supplies pectineus (and the hip joint), not adductor longus.
Adductor longus is supplied by the obturator nerve proper.
The nerve to quadratus femoris is L4, 5, S1 from anterior divisions

The nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1, anterior divisions) also supplies inferior gemellus and the hip joint.
It lies deep to the sciatic nerve.
The inferior gluteal nerve is L5, S1, 2 from posterior divisions

The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) comes from the posterior divisions and supplies gluteus maximus.
It leaves below piriformis.
The superior gluteal nerve comes from anterior divisions

The superior gluteal nerve comes from the posterior divisions (an extensor-type nerve).
L4, L5, S1.
The nerve to obturator internus is L4, 5, S1

The nerve to obturator internus is L5, S1 and S2, not L4, L5, S1.
The nerve to quadratus femoris is L4, L5, S1.
The ilioinguinal is the collateral branch of the iliohypogastric

Last's describes the ilioinguinal nerve as the collateral branch of the iliohypogastric, running parallel at a lower level.
Both are L1.
The ilioinguinal supplies the anterior third of the scrotum

The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the anterior third of the scrotum (or labium) and the root of the penis.
L1 territory.
The iliohypogastric pierces the external oblique aponeurosis 5 cm above the superficial ring

The iliohypogastric nerve pierces the external oblique aponeurosis about 2.5 cm above the superficial ring, not 5 cm.
It supplies the suprapubic skin.
The ilioinguinal enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring

The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal from the side, by piercing internal oblique, not through the deep ring.
It is not in the spermatic cord.
C1, C7, C8, L4 and L5 posterior rami give no cutaneous supply

The posterior rami of C1, C7, C8, L4 and L5 supply muscles but no skin.
So no dorsal dermatomes for these.
Medial branches supply skin in the upper part of the trunk

In the upper part of the trunk the medial branches of the posterior rami supply the skin; in the lower part the lateral branches do.
A Last's principle.
T12 is the dividing level between medial and lateral cutaneous branches

The change from medial to lateral cutaneous branches occurs at about T6, not T12.
Above T6 medial; below lateral.
All lumbar posterior rami supply skin

L4 and L5 posterior rami give no cutaneous supply; not all lumbar posterior rami supply skin.
L1 to L3 do.
It may arise from the femoral nerve in the iliac fossa

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve may arise from the femoral nerve in the gutter between psoas and iliacus.
Otherwise directly from L2 and L3.
It lies in a tunnel about 1 cm medial to the ASIS

It passes into the thigh in a tunnel in or under the inguinal ligament about 1 cm medial to the ASIS, a site of entrapment (meralgia paraesthetica).
Tight belts and obesity are causes.
Its anterior branch is L2

Last's says the anterior branch of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is L3 and the posterior branch L2.
The statement swaps them.
It supplies no peritoneum

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies the parietal peritoneum of the iliac fossa as it crosses it.
So it does supply some peritoneum.
It emerges from the anterior surface of psoas

The genitofemoral nerve emerges from the anterior surface of psoas and runs down on it.
The only branch to do so.
On the left it is crossed by the inferior mesenteric vein

On the left the nerve is crossed by the left colic vessels and the inferior mesenteric vein; on the right by the ileocolic artery.
Retroperitoneal relations.
On the right it is crossed by the inferior mesenteric vein

On the right the genitofemoral nerve is crossed by the ileocolic artery, not the inferior mesenteric vein.
The inferior mesenteric vein is a left-sided structure.
Its femoral branch supplies cremaster

The genital branch supplies cremaster; the femoral branch is sensory to the thigh.
Genital = cremaster.
It lies lateral to the femoral sheath

The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral sheath, separated from the artery.
It is not inside the sheath.
The nerve to vastus medialis is the largest deep branch

The nerve to vastus medialis is the largest deep branch of the femoral nerve and is often double; it also supplies the knee.
It runs in the adductor canal.
The nerve to pectineus runs in front of the femoral sheath

The nerve to pectineus runs behind the femoral sheath, not in front of it.
It passes medially behind the vessels.
The saphenous nerve emerges below the anterior border of sartorius

The saphenous nerve emerges below the posterior border of sartorius, not the anterior border, at the lower end of the adductor canal.
Then it runs with the great saphenous vein.
It emerges from the medial border of psoas

The obturator nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas, lateral to the lumbosacral trunk.
It then runs along the side wall of the pelvis.
Its divisions straddle adductor brevis

The anterior and posterior divisions of the obturator nerve pass in front of and behind adductor brevis.
So they straddle it.
Its posterior division supplies adductor longus

The anterior division supplies adductor longus; the posterior division supplies obturator externus and the adductor part of adductor magnus.
Longus is anterior.
Its anterior division pierces obturator externus

The posterior division pierces obturator externus, not the anterior division.
The anterior division passes above it.
The superior gluteal nerve leaves above piriformis

The superior gluteal nerve and vessels leave the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis; everything else passes below it.
A key landmark.
The superior gluteal nerve ends in tensor fasciae latae

The superior gluteal nerve runs between gluteus medius and minimus, supplying both, and ends in tensor fasciae latae.
Its injury causes a Trendelenburg gait.
The inferior gluteal nerve enters gluteus maximus near its insertion

The inferior gluteal nerve enters gluteus maximus near its origin (the medial end), not near its insertion.
So lateral incisions spare it.
The nerve to quadratus femoris lies superficial to the sciatic nerve

The nerve to quadratus femoris lies deep to the sciatic nerve, against the ischium.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies superficial.
It remains beneath the deep fascia below gluteus maximus

Last's says the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is unique among cutaneous nerves in remaining beneath the deep fascia below gluteus maximus, piercing it only lower down.
It gives branches through the fascia.
Its perineal branch supplies the lateral posterior scrotum

Its perineal branch winds round the hamstring origin to the lateral part of the posterior scrotum or labium; the pudendal nerve supplies the medial part.
A shared territory.
It lies deep to the sciatic nerve

The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies superficial to the sciatic nerve, not deep.
The nerve to quadratus femoris is deep.
It ends at the popliteal fossa

It extends as far as the lower ends of gastrocnemius, beyond the popliteal fossa.
It supplies the back of the thigh and upper calf.
It is supplied by the artery of the sciatic nerve from the inferior gluteal

The sciatic nerve is supplied by the artery of the sciatic nerve from the inferior gluteal artery, the remnant of the embryonic axial artery.
It may persist as a large vessel.
It lies a fingerbreadth lateral to the semimembranosus tendon

In the thigh the sciatic nerve lies about a fingerbreadth lateral to the semimembranosus tendon, under biceps.
A landmark for exposing it.
The tibial part supplies the short head of biceps

The common peroneal part supplies the short head of biceps femoris, not the tibial part.
All other hamstrings are tibial.
When it divides high, the tibial part pierces piriformis

When the sciatic nerve divides high, it is the peroneal part that pierces piriformis.
The tibial part passes below it.
It has no muscular branches apart from a few fibres to tibialis anterior

Last's says the common peroneal nerve has no muscular branches of its own apart from a few fibres to tibialis anterior via the recurrent genicular nerve.
Its muscles are supplied by its terminal branches.
The recurrent genicular nerve supplies the superior tibiofibular joint

The recurrent genicular nerve supplies the superior tibiofibular joint, the knee and a few fibres of tibialis anterior.
It runs with the recurrent tibial artery.
It divides in the substance of peroneus brevis

The common peroneal nerve divides in the substance of peroneus longus, not peroneus brevis.
Around the neck of the fibula.
The lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf supplies the lower half of the peroneal compartment

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf supplies the skin over the upper half of the peroneal compartment, not the lower half.
The superficial peroneal supplies the lower part.

questions.s: The deep and superficial peroneal nerves (Last's):
o: The deep peroneal nerve supplies the skin of the first cleft

The deep peroneal nerve gives cutaneous supply only to the first web space (cleft) between the great and second toes.
A small but diagnostic patch.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies both peronei

The superficial peroneal nerve supplies both peronei, longus and brevis.
It is the nerve of the lateral compartment.
The deep peroneal nerve lies medial to the dorsalis pedis artery

On the dorsum of the foot the deep peroneal nerve lies lateral to the dorsalis pedis artery; the EHL tendon is medial to the artery.
"Tendon, artery, nerve" from medial to lateral.
The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the fascia one-third down the leg

The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the deep fascia about halfway down the leg, not one-third.
It then divides into medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves.
It passes beneath the fibrous arch of soleus

The tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels pass deep to the fibrous arch of soleus into the deep calf.
The arch protects them.
It divides behind the medial malleolus beneath the flexor retinaculum

Behind the medial malleolus, under the flexor retinaculum, the tibial nerve divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves (the tarsal tunnel).
Entrapment here causes tarsal tunnel syndrome.
The sural nerve runs medial to the small saphenous vein at the ankle

At the ankle the sural nerve runs lateral to the small saphenous vein, behind the lateral malleolus.
Not medial.
The medial calcanean nerve supplies the lateral heel

The medial calcanean nerve supplies the weight-bearing skin of the heel (medial and plantar), not the lateral heel.
The lateral heel is sural.
The medial plantar nerve supplies the first lumbrical

The medial plantar nerve supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical, like the median nerve in the hand.
Four muscles.
The deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve supplies adductor hallucis

The deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve supplies adductor hallucis, the lateral three lumbricals and most interossei, like the deep ulnar nerve.
A close parallel.
The medial plantar artery lies lateral to the nerve

The medial plantar artery lies medial to the medial plantar nerve, not lateral.
In the hand the ulnar artery lies lateral to the nerve; in the foot the relation is reversed.
The superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve supplies the three lateral lumbricals

The deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve supplies the three lateral lumbricals, not the superficial branch.
The superficial branch supplies flexor digiti minimi brevis and some interossei.

questions.s: Concerning dorsalis pedis and some small nerves (Last's):
o: The anterior tibial becomes dorsalis pedis midway between the malleoli

The anterior tibial artery becomes dorsalis pedis in front of the ankle, midway between the malleoli.
A landmark for the pulse.
Dorsalis pedis lies between EHL tendon and the deep peroneal nerve

Dorsalis pedis lies between the EHL tendon medially and the deep peroneal nerve laterally, where its pulse is felt.
It is absent in about 10 percent.
The nerve to quadratus femoris supplies superior gemellus

The nerve to quadratus femoris supplies inferior gemellus; the nerve to obturator internus supplies superior gemellus.
Each gemellus goes with the neighbouring muscle.
The perineal branch of S4 supplies the external anal sphincter

The perineal branch of S4 supplies parts of levator ani and coccygeus, and perianal skin, not the external anal sphincter (which is supplied by the inferior rectal nerve).
Last's detail.
